primitives.name: Possession Recoverability
primitives.verbatim_quote: Eleven men make up a football team now, as in the early days of the game, but modern requirements make it necessary that these eleven men play constantly to one end.
primitives.assumptions: Recovery is inversely proportional to team coordination and directly proportional to field distance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When T_{recover} > D_{field}/V_{team}, possession is lost.

layer2.mapping: Possession recoverability mirrors control theory's feedback loop efficiency in distributed systems.

The foundational structure of football emerges from the interplay between individual agency and collective action. The first primitive, 'Team Effort Coherence', formalizes how individual exertions must align into a unified system where E_team = f(E_ind, C), with C representing the degree of synchronization among players. This is not merely additive; rather, it reflects a multiplicative synergy that amplifies or dampens individual contributions. The second primitive, 'Pass Accuracy Dependence', introduces a dependency model where the efficacy of a kicker's action is conditioned upon prior pass quality, modeled as P(A_kick | A_pass). This creates a cascading effect in strategic planning. The third primitive, 'Possession Recoverability', captures the temporal and spatial dynamics of ball control, where recovery time is a function of team velocity and field distance. These primitives form a triadic framework: individual capability (E_ind), conditional reliance (A_pass), and systemic responsiveness (T_recover). Failure modes occur when any component degrades below critical thresholds—when C approaches zero, team performance collapses; when A_pass drops below a minimum, even elite kickers fail; and when T_recover exceeds a latency limit, possession is lost. Each primitive operates within a shared phase space defined by game state variables, enabling cross-layer validation and predictive modeling.
